rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s power, mercy, wisdom, sustenance, and graciousness require a day when He fully administers justice; without it, His evident attributes would be refuted.
rows.anchor: These attributes entail that He bring forth a day in which He administer justice between mankind

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pairing of created things points to a wise creator above the universe who governs its parts and brings them into harmony.
rows.anchor: a wise and sagacious being has created this world; He is above and beyond this universe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The paired nature of creation points to the Hereafter as this world’s counterpart, completing its purpose; without the Hereafter, worldly life is meaningless.
rows.anchor: it is essential that this world also have a counterpart so that its deficiency be compensated by it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the Hereafter is certain, people should leave hostility to God’s messenger, hasten to God, and prepare for accountability, when no one can benefit another.
rows.anchor: when everyone will be held accountable for his deeds and when no one except God will be of any benefit to anyone

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is God’s open warner so no one can claim no warning came; he warns of the Hereafter’s events, leaving people responsible for the consequences.
rows.anchor: so that on that day no one will have the excuse that no warner came to inform them of it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word minhu means the Prophet was specially sent by God to warn his people.
rows.anchor: signifies the fact that the Prophet (sws) has specially been sent by God to warn his people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some people take minhu as a preposition governed by nadhīr, but the author rejects this syntax as contrary to Arabic principles and parallel Qur’anic verses.
rows.anchor: this opinion is against linguistic principles of Arabic as well as parallel verses of the Qur’ān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to set up no deity beside God adds a warning: alleged deities and intercessors cannot rescue people from God’s grasp on Judgement Day.
rows.anchor: their alleged deities and intercessors will save them from God’s grasp

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an repeatedly joins monotheism with the Hereafter to disprove the polytheists’ notion that their deities could intercede for them.
rows.anchor: the Qur’ ān always mentions the belief of monotheism with the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should not grieve: earlier nations treated their messengers the same way, so he is neither uniquely opposed nor negligent in his duty.
rows.anchor: previous nations too have adopted the same attitude with their respective messengers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusations are stock excuses: people called messengers sorcerers when shown signs and possessed when warned of the Hereafter’s punishment.
rows.anchor: when they were warned of the punishment of the Hereafter, they were regarded as men possessed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Like earlier messengers, the Prophet should persevere resolutely through the opposition and fabricated stories directed at him.
rows.anchor: with perseverance, he should combat the circumstances he is facing the way previous messengers did so with resoluteness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author expresses amazement that every generation seems to pass down a will instructing its successors to oppose messengers in the same way.
rows.anchor: it is as if the miscreants of every nation have made a will to the ones who will come later

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The real cause of the Quraysh’s similarity to earlier rejecters is their shared rebellious character, which leads them to the same fate.
rows.anchor: the real cause of this similarity in attitude is that these people [the Quraysh] also are rebellious

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is told to turn away from the hostile people: he has warned and conveyed the truth, so he is not accountable for their rejection; they themselves are to blame.
rows.anchor: he has discharged his responsibility as a messenger of warning them and communicating to them the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the Prophet should ignore the rebellious leaders, he must keep guiding those willing to listen; reminders benefit people seeking faith.
rows.anchor: he should continue to guide those who are ready to listen to him. The seekers of faith benefit from his reminders and instruction

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The order to ignore applies to conceited Quraysh leaders unwilling to listen; the Prophet had pursued them because their conversion might strengthen the new faith and bring others to it.
rows.anchor: the directive of ignoring people relates to the rebellious leaders of the Quraysh who because of conceit were not prepared to listen to anything

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the truth had been conclusively conveyed and the leaders proved immovable, God stopped the Prophet from spending more time pursuing them.
rows.anchor: when the truth had been conclusively conveyed to them, and it became evident that these rocks will not budge from their place

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God created jinn and humans to worship and obey Him, gaining the blessings and rank He has appointed; He does not need to pamper them.
rows.anchor: their purpose of serving and worshipping the one and only God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author reassures believers that God will provide in ways neither they nor their enemies can anticipate and that His schemes are well-grounded.
rows.anchor: It is God alone Who provides and nourishes all and His schemes are very well-grounded

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This reassures Muhammad and his companions amid plans to drive them from Mecca and impose a financial embargo: God alone provides and no enemy can defeat His power.
rows.anchor: the disbelievers were planning to dislodge them from Makkah and impose a financial embargo on them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human responsibility is to serve and worship God; providing for them is God’s responsibility, and He is fully able to do so.
rows.anchor: The obligation of human beings is to serve and worship their Lord

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author links this assurance to Qur’anic instructions to maintain prayer without demanding provision and not covet disbelievers’ worldly gifts.
rows.anchor: Some examples of such verses are given below

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship here broadly means worshipping God and obeying His directives; it is the life purpose people must live and die for and the route to human elevation.
rows.anchor: worshipping God and obeying His directives

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humanity needs worship for its own elevation; those who abandon it sink below the status of animals.
rows.anchor: the stairway to their own elevation is this worship

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jinn and humans are equally endowed with free will and accountability and can attain the same reward and rank through worship.
rows.anchor: both are equally accountable before God and will deserve the same reward and rank

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God has neither assigned creatures the duty of providing for Him or His creation nor needs to be fed; He alone provides and sustains them.
rows.anchor: He has neither imposed on them the responsibility of providing for His creatures

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person’s effort to provide for a family is only a means; God alone makes the effort bear fruit, as the author illustrates from 56:63–64.
rows.anchor: It is only God who causes his efforts to bear fruit

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that God does not want creatures to feed Him refutes polytheists’ belief that their deities consume sacrificial animals.
rows.anchor: a refutation of a false notion of polytheist nations whereby they thought their deities consume and relish the animal sacrifice presented to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adverse circumstances should not cause doubt in God’s providence: He provides for all, and opposition cannot defeat His well-grounded schemes.
rows.anchor: Adverse circumstances and resistance from people cannot defeat His schemes

rows.speaker: Imām Farāhī
rows.claim: Because waqf is made at matīn, its declension is unknown and no recitation difference arises, though a question about declension still remains.
rows.anchor: Since there is a stoppage ( waqf) at the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Farāhī notes that quwwa denotes a rope strand and matīn commonly means the rope’s strength.
rows.anchor: a very common word to signify the strength of a rope

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: One grammatical reading makes matīn genitive as an adjective of quwwa.
rows.anchor: Some regard it to be declined in the genitive and thus an attribute of the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Farāhī answers the gender mismatch by noting that the form faʿīl can be used for either masculine or feminine, as in the verse about God’s mercy being near.
rows.anchor: in Arabic is used both for masculine and feminine genders

rows.speaker: Some other people
rows.claim: Another grammatical reading makes matīn nominative as a qualifier of dhū al-quwwa.
rows.anchor: Some other people regard it to be declined in the nominative qualifying

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Farāhī argues for an implicit subject for matīn because the word is not elsewhere used as a divine attribute; the readings then differ only in inflection, not meaning.
rows.anchor: nowhere else in the Qur’ ān has the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhanūb first means a bucket filled with water, then acquired the figurative sense of a share.
rows.anchor: denotes a filled bucket. It is not used for any empty bucket

rows.speaker: Abū Zu’ayd
rows.claim: Abū Zu’ayd’s couplet uses dhanūb for death’s allotted share among the sons of every father, illustrating the word’s figurative sense.
rows.anchor: A couplet of Abū Zu’ayd reads

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh leaders, like the earlier ʿĀd and Thamūd, have been granted a limited respite for the truth to be conclusively conveyed; they should not demand the punishment early.
rows.anchor: in a similar manner, God has also granted the Quraysh a time of respite

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning of destruction addresses Quraysh disbelievers who taunt the Prophet by demanding punishment before they will believe; that day will bring severe, inescapable ruin.
rows.anchor: while regarding the warnings of the Prophet (sws) to be mere bluff were demanding the punishment merely to pester the Prophet (sws)

none: Closing formula, place, and date only.

rows.speaker: Some people
rows.claim: Some classify Sūrah al-Raḥmān as Madinan.
rows.anchor: Some people have regarded this sūrah to be Madīnan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects a Madinan classification, arguing that no verse appears to be Madinan and the whole sūrah shares one tone and rhythm.
rows.anchor: a single verse of it appears to be Mad īnan much less the whole sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah’s Makkan opponents demand a punishment sign before accepting that rejection brings punishment and everlasting humiliation in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: his opponents, in their fury to refute him, had become adamant on a demand: unless a sign of punishment was shown to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated refrains answer stubborn or obtuse listeners; the recurring verse is contextually embedded and rhetorically apt, despite critics calling it needless repetition.
rows.anchor: at every instance the recurring verse is fully embedded in its context the way a pearl is embedded in a ring

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding Sūrah al-Qamar taught Quraysh to learn from messengers and their history rather than insist on seeing punishment; revelation itself is a favor for education and remembrance.
rows.anchor: In Sūrah al-Qamar, the obdurate people of the Quraysh were told to learn a lesson from messengers and the history of their people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God taught the Qur’an out of mercy; granting speech means humans can understand and teach one another, so they should use this exalted ability for instruction rather than punishment.
rows.anchor: It is the merciful nature of the Almighty because of which He has taught them the Qur’ ān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rather than demand a new sign, opponents should reflect on the familiar signs of the heavens, earth, and the worlds within and around them, which teach the Qur’an’s lesson.
rows.anchor: why do not they deliberate on the signs of the heavens and the earth and the world found inside man and that outside him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Farāhī’s poetry evidence shows that ālāʾ has a broad sense including favours, power, majesty, signs, miracles, marvels, and feats, rather than a single meaning.
rows.anchor: this word is not merely used to mean “favours;” it has a much wider connotation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Farāhī does not deny “favours” as a meaning but rejects treating it as the word’s only meaning; the author says his analysis is often used without proper attribution.
rows.anchor: contest that the meaning of this word is “favours;” however, he does contest that this

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Farāhī explains that earlier scholars specified a word’s contextual use when answering a question, rather than defining its full lexical range.
rows.anchor: They would specify that at a particular instance

rows.speaker: All the exegetes
rows.claim: Exegetes unanimously take the dual-addressed refrain to address both humans and jinn.
rows.anchor: All the exegetes are unanimous that the verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author finds it difficult to say Muhammad was sent to the jinn or conclusively conveyed the message to them, since a prophet’s language, representative nature, and exemplary life fit his own people.
rows.anchor: it is difficult to say that the Prophet (sws) was also sent towards the jinn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet may have encountered jinn who heard some Qur’an and liked it, but he learned of their response through revelation; such meetings do not amount to conclusive delivery.
rows.anchor: a group of jinn had heard a few verses of the Qur’ ān from the blessed tongue of the Prophet (sws) and liked them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah’s address can reach inattentive jinn through the Qur’an’s mercy on shared principles such as monotheism, resurrection, reward, punishment, truth, and justice, though jinn are not its direct addressees.
rows.anchor: the mercy of the Qur’ān at times extends to the jinn – specially in those matters of principle which are common between them and man

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because jinn have free will and accountability, the author infers that God must have sent prophets and messengers from among them, speaking their language; this fits divine practice and no Qur’anic verse contradicts it.
rows.anchor: it is essential as per the practice of God for their guidance, prophets and messengers must have been sent to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author cites the plural command to Adam and Satan and the promise of future guidance as Qur’anic support for guidance reaching both kinds of beings.
rows.anchor: both of them are addressed at the end in the following words
